newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-BLACKER BOK TEAM WOULD BE BETTER, CRITICS SAY.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-BLACKER BOK TEAM WOULD BE BETTER, CRITICS SAY.

text.p: South African rugby fans found themselves on Monday in a depressingly familiar state of mind -- agonised introspection over why their team keeps losing.

Fresh from a disastrous 1996 season of losses against New Zealand and Australia, the Springboks went down on Saturday to a series defeat by the British Lions, who have now won two tests with one to go.

Before the Lions arrived, they had been widely written off in South Africa as a plucky but ultimately doomed side who would only confirm the dominance of southern hemisphere rugby over the game as played in the north.
But in the event the Lions showed up the failings of a Springbok side which has had two changes in coach since the brief glory of the 1995 World Cup plus a dozen switches in personnel.
South African commentators on Monday blamed the team's defeat on everything including the lack of a reliable place kicker, arrogance and even their failure to select black players.
"End of rugby's big white lie," ran the main front page headline in the Cape Times.
"The country's Rugby World Cup victory only served to perpetuate the myth of the lilywhite Springboks' supremacy," the paper's rugby writer said.
In a another editorial, the paper told Louis Luyt, president of the South African Rugby Football Union, to "join the new South Africa".
"There have been some ridiculously racist suggestions that maybe blacks are not meant to be playing rugby," the paper said, referring to the all-white make-up of the current Springbok squad.
"And when (blacks) can play, some racists seem to think that they are suitable only for back-line positions."
Without mentioning names, the Afrikaans-language Die Burger said in an editorial headlined "Springbok trauma" that the problem might be that SARFU's leadership was too dictatorial.
"Before the players are blamed, the rugby bosses must first study their own hearts. The dictatorial way the game is managed at top level will eventually take its toll, as is happening now."
The paper also lamented the absence of someone who could kick the ball between the posts, a lack which cost the side a potential 15 points and a winning margin in Saturday's second test in Durban.
The Cape Argus called on Luyt to quit

"The point when South African rugby started to go downhill can be measured almost to the minute. It was when Luyt made his boastful speech...a day after the Springboks won the World Cup," the paper said in an editorial.

Luyt had claimed, much to the annoyance of New Zealand and Australia, that if South Africa had not been isolated from world rugby and banned from playing in the first two competitions, the Springboks would have been completing a hat-trick of wins.
The rest of the season promises a good deal more unhappy introspection for Springbok supporters -- the next opponents their team faces are the All Blacks and the Wallabies.
